newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Exiled Cambodian prince due to be jailed on return.
newsitem.headline: Exiled Cambodian prince due to be jailed on return.

text.p: Cambodia's exiled Prince Norodom Sirivudh, accused of plotting to kill co-Premier Hun Sen, will be taken to prison if he returns home as planned on Tuesday, a top government official said.

"If he arrives he will be taken to T3 (prison in Phnom Penh). That's what we plan to do," co-Interior Minister You Hockry told Reuters on Tuesday, while confirming that Sirivudh had boarded a Hong Kong-bound flight in Frankfurt on Monday.

You Hockry, a royalist, said he had discussed the issue on Sunday with co-minister Sar Kheng of Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP), which formed an uneasy coalition with the royalist FUNCINPEC party after U.N.-run elections in 1993.
"Sirivudh must come with a pardon. Without a royal pardon FUNCINPEC cannot do much legally," said the minister.
Hun Sen has warned of possible dire consequences if Sirivudh returns.
The streets of Phnom Penh were quiet early on Tuesday, the middle of the three-day Cambodian New Year holiday. Sirivudh was not expected until late afternoon on a flight from Hong Kong.

Sirivudh, former foreign minister and half brother of King Norodom Sihanouk, was sent into exile in December 1995 after being held for one month on charges of involvement in an alleged plot against the life of the second prime minister.
Sirivudh has denied the charges against him and has said he wants to return to seek justice.

His support group in Paris issued a statement on Monday saying he would be returning to his homeland on Tuesday despite appeals from FUNCINPEC officials, including co-Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, to postpone his plans at a time of tense relations within the government.

There has been speculation that foreign legislators would accompany Sirivudh but the Cambodia Daily newspaper on Tuesday quoted his sister, Princess Vacheara, as saying in Paris that he would be alone.
Sihanouk said last week he was not ready to make an enemy of Hun Sen by granting an amnesty and warned that he would abdicate immediately if the Sirivudh affair was settled by violence.
Strongman Hun Sen has consistently refused to back a royal pardon for Sirivudh, who was jailed 10 years in absentia for the plot, and warned of violence if he returns.

He said last week that the prince was "the spark that could create fire", while warning people to avoid Phnom Penh's Pochentong Airport when he returns and saying royalists should not try to prevent his arrest.
A diplomat, asked about the potential for trouble, said: "We don't know if he will be allowed to get off the plane."

An aide to Hun Sen, Om Yentieng, told Reuters on Tuesday he did not expect trouble and believed Sirivudh would be taken to the run-down French colonial-era T3 prison. "I don't think FUNCINPEC is against the law," he said.

FUNCINPEC called last month on the king to grant Sirivudh an amnesty and some fear his return could stoke tensions between the two parties after a deadly March 30 grenade attack on a protest led by opposition leader and FUNCINPEC ally, Sam Rainsy.
Nineteen people were killed and 100 people injured when unknown assailants threw four grenades at a crowd of 150-200 people outside parliament in Phnom Penh.

Co-Premier Ranariddh, who is also King Sihanouk's son, left for Thailand on Monday and senior members of his cabinet were unable to say when he would be back, although one said it would not be on Tuesday.
